paras: The mobbing of the Armstrong County temperance attorney was a street confrontation in Armstrong County, Pennsylvania, in March 1888, in which a crowd surrounded the lawyer for the county's temperance party. He was rescued by several citizens and, in the words of the only report found, "escaped lynching"; no one was reported hurt.

In March 1888 Pennsylvania courts were hearing liquor-license applications, and a Pittsburg dispatch counted more than 700 remonstrances against licenses in Allegheny County alone. Armstrong County, according to the same dispatch, was "greatly excited" over Judge Neal's decision annulling all licenses in the county, which meant prohibition there for at least a year.

During the license proceedings, the attorney for the temperance side had suggested to the court that the eighty people who signed one saloon keeper's petition were not respectable. The dispatch noted that several women had signed that petition. Some time before March 15 the attorney was surrounded on a street by what the report called "an angry mob" and was rescued from the crowd by "several well-known citizens". The report did not name the attorney, the town, the day or anyone in the crowd.
No report of arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The incident appeared on the front page of the New-York Tribune of March 16, 1888, in a Pittsburg special headlined "An Exciting Temperance Crusade" with the subhead "An Attorney Mobbed". The mob took up two sentences at the end of a report mostly about license remonstrances and the arrival of General Lew Wallace's mother to join the anti-saloon campaign. The Tribune made no comment on the crowd, and race was not mentioned.
No other paper carrying the story was found.

accounts.label: Pittsburg special to the New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: Amid excitement over Judge Neal's annulment of all licenses, the temperance attorney was surrounded by an angry mob and escaped lynching when rescued by several well-known citizens, after he had told the court that a saloon keeper's eighty petitioners were not respectable.

framing.detail: Headlined 'AN EXCITING TEMPERANCE CRUSADE' with the subhead 'AN ATTORNEY MOBBED'; the mob incident is two sentences in a report on license remonstrances, with no comment on the mob.

record_check.dossier: Mob confrontation (threatened lynching) with no killing; mob_assault rather than lynching.
Supported: Armstrong County in a Pittsburg dispatch about Pennsylvania license courts.
Race not stated; the target was the temperance party's attorney, and nothing in the report frames the incident racially.
Before March 15, 1888 (date of the dispatch); exact date not given.
No crime alleged; the provocation reported was his remark to the court about the saloon petitioners.
